Women organizations have established a presence in the community and have worked through cultural and educational initiatives alongside with the Abuelas and the community leaderships. Once ostracized, the Abuelas represent now hope. Their leadership is recognized and praised by the community, from children to ancestral authorities and the Guatemalan society at large. However, there is much to be done in the compliance of the reparation sentence. In the Abuelas' words, the responsible institutions need to to ensure the full exercise of their rights and those of their communities, including the realms of education, housing, or land ownership. They also have asked the Congress to pass a law to recognize the 26th of February as the National Day of Justice for Conflict-Related Sexual Violence. The Abuelas requested us to convey one Last key message: Advocate for transformative reparations for crimes of conflict-related sexual violence. We ask all of you to advocate for the implementation of the Sepur Zarco sentence so that reparations become a reality for everyone and justice can finally be served.

Thank you so much, Abuelas de Sepur Zarco, for sharing your lived experience. It's important that your legacy is carried on throughout generations. And heartfelt thanks to UN Women Guatemala and Mujeres Transformando el Mundo for your support in putting together this video. I am now pleased to introduce Ms. Lucia Di Pascal Solage, who is the founder and general coordinator of the feminist organization Neges Mawan in Haiti.

Thank you so much, Excellencies. Ladies and gentlemen, Haiti is facing a multidimensional crisis. For the first 3 months of the year, more than 1,000 people were killed and over 1.3 million have been displaced. More than half of whom are women and girls. Thousands of women and girls have been raped, left without justice, without care, many contracting sexually transmitted infection or becoming pregnant from the assault. Suffering in silence. Sexual violence, especially collective rape, has become a strategic weapon of war used by armed gangs to terrorize and control entire communities. Watching this video of this survivor have been remind me the documentary Les Enfants du Coup d'État by the Haitian filmmaker Rachel Magloire. It is a powerful film that share the voices of Haitian women survivors who were raped during the military coup between 1991 and 1994. These women were forced to carry pregnancies resulting from rape in a country where abortion is completely criminalized. I also recall the stories of Haitian women who were subjected to systematic sexual violence during the Duvalier dictatorship. Rape was also used as a colonial tool of domination and dehumanization of Haitian women and girls, dates black to to slavery, when the sexual violence against enslaved Black women was institutionalized to uphold systems of control and exploitation. These crimes leave more than physical wounds. They create deep individual and collective trauma, trauma that are passed from one generation to another. And yet healing remains inaccessible because justice is denied, support systems are underfunded, and feminist culturally grounded response are absent or ignored. So yes, as an Asian woman, an Asian feminist, and a survivor of sexual violence myself, I know the importance of breaking the cycle, healing the scars, and addressing the intergenerational effect of this violence. Feminist organizations, especially in the Global South, have created powerful models of response and recovery rooted in survivors' lived experiences, our cultures, and our resilience. These approaches are beyond trauma care. They center dignity, reclaim power, and restore autonomy. In our feminist organization, by example, in Haiti, Neges Mawo, our program Sisterhood embodies that vision of survivor-centered sorority and healing. Feminist organizations have also pushed for active for effective response to gender-based violence, and for centering women's leadership and rights, I prioritize in confronting conflict. And yet, in addressing Haiti's present and past crisis, Haitian women have consistently been invisibilized. This failure is shocking because the UN and its member states have concluded that centering women is necessary to resolving conflict through UN Security Council resolution 1325 and its progeny. Resolution 1820, for example, acknowledges explicitly that sexual violence used as a tool of conflict threatens peace and must be addressed as a peacebuilding priority. The Women, Peace and Security Agenda created by this resolution makes clear that addressing sexual violence and centering women's leadership are not optional. They are critical to ending conflict and building lasting peace for home— addressing— doing social and economic prosperity. By example, for almost a year, Haitian feminists have been involved in promoting the policy framework for an effective and equitable transition in Haiti, an initiative put forward by Haitian civil society with global solidarity support in response to Haiti's women and girls being yet again left behind, even as they are targeted with brutal violence. The framework offers specific recommendations for urgent action. In the absence of that action, Haiti's crisis has only grown worse. While violence is intensifying globally, we are also witnessing the rise of fascism, extremist nationalism, racism, and sexism, further escalating the risk faced by women and girls while attempting to roll back decades of hard-won rights. We cannot resolve the problems of today by erasing the mistakes of yesterday. Asian women and women across the world cannot heal and will not be safe if we continue to apply the same harmful actions that silence them, marginalize them, and deny them agency. Women are survivors, organizers, community builders, and changemakers. We must stop erasing them, we must stop silencing them, and we must stop framing them only as passive victims. We have always been on the frontline and we will continue to be. We are working to influence global policies and to shape the response we need. This means including survivors and feminist organizations in decision-making processes, funding allocation, policy design, and implementation. It requires adopting an intersectional and decolonial approach. It requires empowering feminist approach like the policy framework. Our knowledge and voices must be placed at the center of doable and transformative solution if we want to see a peaceful and thriving world for all. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Miss Solange, for channeling your personal pain into an inspiring and teaching moment for us, and for highlighting the importance of speaking up against injustice for survivors everywhere, especially in your home country, Haiti, but for survivors around the world. I am very pleased now to hand the floor to the Director of Programme Policy and Intergovernmental Division of UN Women, Ms. Sarah Hendricks on behalf of the UN Action Network. Hi, Sarah.

Thank you very much. And indeed, thank you for this important moment today. To Ambassador Tropepi, to SRSJ-PATIN, to the Office of SRSJ-Gamba, Mr. Bryce Pease, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and friends around this important table, Fellow advocates who are here, the International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict is certainly a day that demands action. It is a day to confront the truth that conflict-related sexual violence is not collateral damage. It is, in fact, calculated, systematic, and devastating weapon of war, as we have heard from so many testimonies today. The testimonies across today's time together are not actually isolated stories. They are in fact part of a much larger, more brutal design repeated across countries, repeated across contexts, and certainly across generations. One that is shaped by impunity and also shaped by silence and shaped in fact by the absence of justice. This. These stories, however, as we've heard today, are also threaded with resistance. Survivors have and are speaking out, have spoken out, not just because this is safe or easy. In fact, far too many times it is nothing but that, but because they refuse to let this pain go ignored. They build care where none exists and carry truths institutions have far too long failed to hold. And yet, too often, we ask survivors to carry this burden alone. Today must be a day not just of symbolic remembrance, but in fact a day of defiance and concrete accountability, because every act of brutality and every tactic of fear is met far too many times, again and again, by those who choose to speak, to organize, and to insist on something more than survival. This year's theme, the deep and lasting intergenerational wounds of conflict-related sexual violence, exposes a brutal truth, and we've heard that already from all of the speakers today, and that brutal truth is that trauma is inherited. When we deny justice, when we silence survivors, when we sentence their children to carry the consequences, this pain is not something that fades. It transforms into fear, into stigma, into poverty, and into violence that has echoes right across generations. Conflict-related sexual violence is not only a personal trauma, it is in fact a political and structural failure. And it continues not because we lack tools, but because we have not matched commitments with the will to act. On behalf of UN Women, we are honored and humbled and proud to respond to conflict-related sexual violence as one of the founding members of the UN Action Against Sexual Violence in Conflict Network, this important network that is chaired by SRSG Patton. UN Action has catalyzed profound normative, but also institutional and operational transformation. The legal documentation and prosecution that has taken place in Ukraine, as well as in many other countries. In Afghanistan and Iraq, we invest in trauma-informed and comprehensive services for survivors. In Eastern Congo, we support women to turn survival into economic independence. Independence, as well as into leadership in their communities. And globally, we advance knowledge to address all aspects of a survivor's healing, their journey, including the intergenerational components of this. And whilst this network has done many important things, we are yet not where we need to be in this work. And you've heard many of these statistics already today, but they bear being repeated. In 2024, just 1.3% of humanitarian aid actually addressed gender-based violence around the world. Only 30% of gender-based violence funding appeals were met, even as conflict has grown disproportionately right around the world. And nearly 90% of women-led frontline organizations remain underfunded, with half facing closure. This is data that is just one month old. I'll say that again: 90% of women-led frontline organizations remain underfunded, with half now facing closure. Mental health services remain chronically neglected. And this is not just a funding gap, it is a protection gap, it is a justice gap, it is in fact a dignity gap. A gap that will not only close with resourced structured survivor-led solidarity, but with a commitment to doing so. And therefore, UN Women joins the voices that have come around today's table, calling on member states and donors to allocate at least 2% of all humanitarian and crisis response aid to the prevention and response to gender-based violence, including conflict-related sexual violence. And to urge the replenishment of the UN Action Trust Fund, which enables coordinated, catalytic, and survivor-centered interventions across the UN system under SRSG Patton's leadership. We also call on governments to strengthen laws that protect against sexual violence, to investigate and prosecute perpetrators, and to provide comprehensive services to survivors. And we call on faith and community leaders to reject silence and indeed to champion dignity. Survivors are not just symbols. They are in fact experts. They are the organizers. They are already leading, as you've heard today, but far too often without recognition or resources and far too often without rest. The least that we can do is to meet their courage with institutional action. So let today be a day where the world stops whispering about wartime rape and starts acting boldly and unapologetically on behalf of every survivor and on behalf of every child in every generation still carrying these unhealed wounds. With this, I thank you.

I thank Ms. Sarah Hendricks for highlighting the importance of coordination in the UN system to address CRSV and for putting the spotlight on the intergenerational consequences of unaddressed harm and honoring the leadership of survivors. I am very pleased now to introduce Ms. Kavya Ahsoka, Executive Director of the NGO Working Group on Women, Peace and Security, Security. The NGO Working Group on Women, Peace and Security is an independent advocacy coalition of 18 civil society organizations that advocates for women's rights.

Thank you so much for that. Thank you, Excellencies, for the opportunity to address you today on behalf of the NGO Working Group and provide a civil society perspective on this important topic of addressing the intergenerational harms of conflict-related sexual violence. Across the world today, we see unprecedented levels of militarization and conflict, with over 600 million women and girls paying the price while they remain sidelined from decision-making on peace and security. The war in Gaza, found to be genocide by Amnesty International, is devastating the lives of all Palestinians, particularly women and girls. More than 28,000 women and girls have been killed since October 2023. Country with a woman and girl killed every hour. The COI not only detailed how these violations have caused severe immediate suffering to women and girls, but have resulted in irreversible long-term harm to Palestinians as a group. These violations are being carried out before our eyes with complete disregard for international humanitarian and human rights law. In Sudan, the same forces who perpetrated a genocide in Darfur 20 years ago are once again responsible for widespread widespread atrocities. Women and girls have been subjected to sexual violence by all warring parties, including kidnapping, rape, and sexual slavery. And women and girls from non-Arab tribes, particularly in Darfur, have been targeted due to their ethnicity. And yet, in the face of this brutality, as USG Fletcher said last week, Sudan has become a grim example of the twin themes of this moment: indifference and impunity. And in Afghanistan, the Taliban's systematic erasure of women and girls from public life, banning them from accessing education, healthcare, and basic services, and even from speaking in public or looking out the window, will reverberate for generations. While Afghan women continue to bravely resist these policies and demand respect for their human rights, the international community has yet to hold the Taliban accountable for their crimes against humanity or ensure that Afghan women are meaningfully included in decision-making about their own future. All these examples point to a simple fact: violations of the human rights of women and girls, including acts of conflict-related sexual violence, continue in these contexts and far too many others precisely because perpetrators know that they will likely be able to get away with it. Laws mean nothing if they are not enforced. Words mean nothing if they are not backed by action. As Afghan human rights defender Azada Razmohammad told the Security Council in March, "If impunity is the disease, accountability is the only antidote." Holistic, gender-sensitive, survivor-centered accountability that prioritizes women's agency, bodily autonomy, human rights, and participation is crucial in both addressing the harms of conflict today and preventing future generations from experiencing these atrocities in the future. This year we commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Women, Peace and Security Agenda. When we should be celebrating the gains of feminist movements and the courage and leadership of women human rights defenders in conflicts and crises, we are instead witnessing an alarming backlash against women's autonomy and rights. The very term gender a core concept in international human rights law and used by feminist movements for decades to challenge biological determinism and the systematic oppression of women and LGBTQI people, is today being blatantly undermined by anti-gender movements. If we believe in the norms, institutions, including this mandate and commitments of 25 years of the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, if we all believe that all forms of gender-based violence and gender inequality are unacceptable. You all—member states, Security Council members, and UN leadership—must uphold these norms and defend these institutions today when the stakes could not be higher, or risk losing them entirely. As MSF said earlier this week about Gaza, every delay, every equivocation, and every policy that permits the machinery of devastation To roll forward with impunity is an act of complicity. This applies as much to the millions of women and girls confronting the brutal realities of conflict. They need your advocacy, they need your resources, but most importantly, your political courage and moral clarity that their rights are not dispensable. Thank you.

You could have gone on for another 5 minutes, I would have allowed it. Thank you, Miss Asoka, for emphasizing the importance of women's participation in all aspects of the fight against conflict-related sexual violence. To the screen we go.

Dear friends, as the Global Champion in the fight against conflict-related sexual violence and Youth Liaison to SRSG Office, I speak from a generation that refuses to inherit silence. Conflict-related sexual violence is a wound that doesn't close when the war ends. It echoes through generations, it lingers in the bodies of survivors, in the memories passed down, in the shame imposed by society. And yet, through all of this, survivors rise. Youth rise. Young people are not removed from this story. Young people are born into it, into these histories, sometimes spoken, often silenced. Young people carry the weights of inherited trauma, often without explanation, without justice, without healing, but also carry the power to transform it and to demand change. Today's theme, Breaking the Silence, Healing the Scars: Addressing the Intergenerational Effects of Conflict-Related Sexual Violence, calls us to action. It reminds us that healing is not passive. It is political. It is personal. It is intergenerational. Many young people are survivors themselves. Others are children born of rape. Living with unanswered questions, stolen origins. Their voices are too often left out of the conversation, and that must change. We are a generation that will say, "This ends with us." To every survivor, every young person who has carried this pain without words, I see you. You are not alone. Your healing is revolutionary. Your story is sacred, and your voice is so powerful. So how do we do this? It starts with truth, and it demands courage, the kind of courage that shifts budgets, that reforms institutions, that centers healing instead of hiding. I call on decision makers to match our urgency. Listen to survivors, not as victims but as leaders. Include children born of wartime rape in reparation, justice, and peace processes, not as just dependents but as rights holders. Protect young human rights defenders and frontline responders from retaliation and make space for youth leadership, not as an afterthought but as architects of peace. Young people are not asking for inclusion in the margins. But for shifting the center. Intergenerational trauma requires intergenerational co-leadership. Let me explain what that looks like. One, appoint youth co-leads in the national CRSV strategies and transitional justice processes. Two, mandate intergenerational representation in peace negotiation teams, in truth commissions, in reparation boards. 3, fund youth-led survivor initiatives through multi-year core funding, not project-based microgrants. 4, prioritize data collection on intergenerational trauma, including psychosocial and legal needs of youth born of rape. 5, include young peacebuilders and survivor advocates in Security Council briefings, in field missions. The Youth Peace and Security Agenda, YPS, should not be isolated from conflict-related sexual violence. And 6, support cross-generational healing spaces where storytelling, memory work, collective care are prioritized. Intergenerational co-leadership is not about inviting young people to the table. It's about co-creating the table together where lived experience is leadership, where the future is co-authored by those who bear the scars and those who refuse to repeat them. This is a call for reform, for funding, for political will, for memory, and for healing. Too many of our systems are built to protect perpetrators. We must flip the script from exclusion to co-leadership. This is the world young people are building, and this is the future survivors deserve. Thank you.

Thank you, Aya, for highlighting the role that youth in leadership— the role of youth in leadership in healing intergenerational trauma. We have heard from both grandmothers and now the voice of youth on how they can be a reservoir of hope in the fight against conflict-related sexual violence and the intergenerational trauma it inflicts. So we get into the most exciting part of the programme, member states and regional groups to present their statements. And we start with the European Union, His Excellency Mr. Stavros Lambrinidis, Ambassador Permanent Representative for the EU. Sir.

Dear friends, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states.— and to begin by thanking, of course, the Permanent Mission of Argentina and the officers of the SRSGs for Sexual Violence in Conflict and Children in Armed Conflict for organizing today's event. Friends, sexual violence in conflict remains a horrific tactic of war. People have said this in this room. It doesn't just happen as an afterthought. Across many regions of the globe,— with devastating consequences, not just on individuals but on entire generations. Survivors, their families, children born of wartime rape, and communities are left grappling with trauma, stigma, marginalization. Healing requires recognition and support to the victims, as well as the sustained engagement of communities and institutions that confront these enduring scars. Now, many people have spoken about the necessity to match words with actions, and I fully agree. Now, I think all of you know in this room that the European Union and its member states stand in full solidarity with all survivors of conflict-related violence and their families, particularly children born of rape, and I think you probably all know that we are deeply committed to addressing their needs through protection, physio-social support, socio-economic integration, to break the cycles of trauma and inequality. So, to put it in other words, ending sexual violence in conflict is a core priority of EU foreign policy, and we back this commitment with concrete actions. Now, let me give you an example. The European Union Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security concretely integrates a gender perspective into peacekeeping and humanitarian responses. We are doing this on the ground every day because we have, all of us, committed to ensuring that we put action where our mouth is. We have invested over $8 million in the last 2 years for projects supporting justice, psychosocial care, and sexual and reproductive health care services for CRSV survivors in countries such as Haiti and the Central African Republic. Now, we also have political directions to embassies around the world and to our member states' embassies around the world. We call them guidelines. And we have updated those guidelines on children in armed conflict to better prevent and respond to violations of the rights of the child, including sexual violence, on the ground now in over 150 countries. This is the political commitment of the EU and its member states, and we're acting on it with governments and supporting civil society every day. Now, there's the crisis zones, and then you have beyond crisis zones, and there we tackle gender-based violence globally on the ground through, among other things, the Spotlight Initiative. Now, you do know about that, of course, it's the huge initiative that the European Union has— is running around the world together with the United Nations and the ACT program, but also here in New York as chair of the Group of Friends for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls. I think that's important, colleagues. Many of you have mentioned the issue of political pressure now, political will, as we commemorate this International Day. The center of international politics happens to be New York. We always constantly try to think about how to expand those group of friends to ensure that it's not just a talking shop or an action shop for the converted, but actually brings in more countries, countries who may have nothing against this topic but may not immediately prioritize it or may not feel they have ownership of it. Well, we are trying to give that ownership to countries around the world, here in New York. So the political pressure is huge. Now, at the same time, some— many of you have mentioned impunity. Impunity. Now, it is a scourge, impunity, frankly, and it is as big of a scourge in many ways as the crimes committed themselves, because without— with impunity, nothing stops them. Nothing is there to prevent them. And Again, what are we going to do? Well, we have to strengthen— many of you said— legal procedures at national, regional, international levels. So this is a daily political, diplomatic, and funding priority of the European Union around the world. Finally, colleagues, there are root causes to this. Conflict-related sexual violence is the result of deeply entrenched inequalities and harmful norms. So we are determined to address those root causes, starting by ensuring the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in decision-making at all levels, in all countries around the world, and of course here in New York as well. So you can count us as, you know, the biggest allies of everyone around the world trying to get rid of this scourge, trying to commemorate this International Day effectively, and I hope we can count on you to build together the partnerships that will eventually really push the needle on this. So thank you very much.

I thank the Permanent Representative of the European Union, and just a reminder, folks, 3 minutes. You get 3 minutes each, so you escaped the web of the 3-minute web. Lucky guy. I think we just beat them in the Test cricket, didn't we? At last I know— yes!

Thank you Chair, and I deliver this statement on behalf of Canada, New Zealand, and my own country Australia. Can we thank Argentina for its leadership and commitment to raising awareness of the intergenerational effects of conflict-related sexual violence? Conflict-related sexual violence is a grave violation of human rights and international law. As we've heard this morning it terrorizes populations, fractures communities and perpetuates cycles of trauma. Survivors, including women and girls, men and boys, bear the immediate trauma, but the pain does not end with them. It reverberates across generations, seeping into families, communities, and the very fabric of society, creating a legacy of silence, stigma, and suffering. On this International Day, For the elimination of sexual violence in conflict, we must confront the profound, complex, and long-lasting intergenerational impacts of conflict-related sexual violence. Intergenerational trauma undermines social cohesion and trust, making it harder for communities to heal and rebuild after conflict. Children born of rape may be denied legal identity, nationality, or inheritance rights. This legal invisibility can limit access to education, healthcare, reparations, and protections. Chair, as highlighted in the UN Secretary-General's 2024 report, we're witnessing a disturbing rise in sexual violence in conflict zones, which is likely only the tip of the iceberg. These deliberate and despicable tactics of war are not isolated tragedies. They are systematic failures that demand a systematic response. A systematic response includes strengthening legal frameworks to ensure perpetrators are held accountable through international and domestic legal mechanisms, including the Security Council using all tools at its disposal to prevent and respond to all forms of sexual and gender-based violence. It also means supporting survivor-centered approaches that prioritize dignity, agency, and long-term recovery. By ensuring access to justice, reparations, and services that address the full spectrum of harm, including mental health, education, and economic empowerment. Chair, we must dismantle this— the structural inequalities and gender-based discrimination that enable such violence to occur. We must strengthen early warning systems and invest in conflict prevention and peacebuilding that prioritizes women's meaningful leadership gender equality, and human rights. Prevention is not passive. It requires political will, coordinated action, and survivor-centered approaches. Survivors must be at the heart of our response, not only as recipients of support, but also as agents of change. Their voices, experience, and leadership are essential to breaking the cycle of violence and harm. Let us stand together not only in solidarity with survivors, but in action to ensure that no child, no family, and no community ever has to inherit the scars of war. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador. The next speaker is the Permanent Representative of Albania, Her Excellency Suela Janina. Ambassador, please.

Thank you, Moderator. Thank you, Madam Special Representative, Excellencies, colleagues. The powerful testimonies that we have heard today is yet another reminder that conflict-related sexual violence is not only a heinous crime, it is a strategic weapon of war that tears at the fabric of the entire communities. It is an assault not just on individuals but on generations. The trauma it leaves behind is not contained to a single moment. It goes throughout times, through families, through societies. It sows the seed of stigma, exclusion, poverty, and cycles of violence that, if left undressed, undermine peacebuilding and reconciliation. Colleagues, addressing the impact of CRCV is not only a matter of justice. It is a prerequisite for sustainable peace. It demands that we invest in prevention, protect survivors, and ensure accountability at all levels. Including through national legislation and international cooperation. As a global community, we have a duty to ensure that survivors are no longer silenced by fear or shame. Albania stands in unwavering solidarity with survivors and all those working courageously to break the cycle of violence impunity. I thank the Permanent Representative of Albania, and it is my delight now to give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste, Ambassador Dionisio Babo Soares.

Thank you. All protocols observed. Ladies and gentlemen, echoes of atrocities committed from the World War era where Timorese women were forced into slavery, and through the years of between 2075 and 1999, marked by widespread rape, sexual torture, forced marriages, and mass displacement, and continue to reverberate across generations even until today. This legacy of violence manifests as intergenerational trauma, where the psychological, emotional, and Even biological effects of severe stress experienced by survivors are transmitted through their descendants. Survivors often carry chronic physical ailments and reproductive health issues which can be passed down through neglect, lack of access to care, or genetic predisposition influenced by ancestral stress. Psychologically, symptoms like PTSD, depression, anxiety, chronic grief, and pervasive mistrust common and deeply impacting parenting styles, emotional regulation within families, and the mental health of children who may exhibit behavioral issues or internalize their parents' unresolved pain. Recognizing this immense challenge, not to count the others that have been mentioned here around this table, the Timor-Leste government has tried to address this historical injustice on their and their ongoing impact. Initiatives like the Commission of Truth, Reception and Reconciliation have been crucial in documenting testimonies and promoting reconciliation through implementing complete justice and recommendations, but remains difficult. It was reported that about 30% of women in Timor-Leste suffered the post-traumatic sexual abuse and of any sort of violence several years ago and it still actually has impact until today. So the development of policies protecting survivors of gender-based violence, collaboration with NGOs and also the international partners to provide vital psychosocial support, counseling and trauma-informed care to survivors and families, and empowering communities to lead their healing process, drawing on traditional wisdom, are key national strategies. Aimed at building resilience and fostering support. However, the sheer scale of the trauma and limited resources pose significant challenges, demanding that interventions be both sustained and adaptable to address the long-term natural and intergenerational wounds. So it is our collective moral and ethical obligation to support these issues, and countries like Timor-Leste and others with similar experiences in this healing journey. This critical support is needed for several interconnected reasons. First is that significant sustained funding is essential to expand the— and professionalize trauma healing services, building local capacity and establish long-term support systems. Sharing expertise and trauma-informed care, mental health, restorative justice, and human rights can strengthen local initiatives. To training and developing culturally sensitive approaches. Continued advocacy for justice for survivors, including accountability where possible, and vital symbolic recognition and reparations send a powerful message against impunity, as some have echoed this around this table. Also, in the current situation, integrating trauma-informed approaches into broader government development programs such as education, health, economic development, ensure these initiatives contribute to holistic healing and avoid re-traumatization. And of course, supporting efforts to remember and acknowledge survivors' experiences transform the bitter experiences into a foundation for a more just and peaceful future. So breaking the cycle of intergenerational trauma in countries like Timor-Leste is a monumental task and requiring unwavering commitment. It's time for action, as many have said. I thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste, and I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Malta, Her Excellency Vanessa Fraser.

Thank you, Excellencies, colleagues. I'm honored I am honored to join you in the commemoration of the 11th International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict. Today, we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to preventing conflict-related sexual violence and to supporting survivors across generations. We know that sexual violence in conflict leaves deep, often invisible scars on survivors, but also on their children, families, and communities. The intergenerational effects of such violence, be it through social exclusion, trauma, or lack of access to services, can perpetuate cycles of harm for decades. This is why Malta continues to advocate for survivor-centered, gender-responsive, and trauma-informed approaches. During our Security Council presidency in April 2024, we We place CRSV at the heart of our agenda. We convened the Council's annual open debate on this issue at ministerial level, and we heard powerful testimony from the Secretary-General's Special Representative, Ms. Patton, as well as survivors and civil society leaders, including from Sudan and the Great Lakes region. We also underscored the importance of inclusive participation ensuring the safe engagement of women civil society briefers, and advocating for stronger accountability, including through the use of targeted sanctions against perpetrators of CRSV. Yet justice alone cannot heal the deep wounds of this heinous crime. Survivors require holistic healthcare, including access to mental health and psychosocial services in conflict and post-conflict settings. These services are essential for breaking the cycle of silence and shame that perpetuate, perpetuate trauma across generations. As members of the International Alliance on Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict, Malta remains committing to advancing policies that are inclusive, rights-based, and rooted in the lived experiences of survivors. We are also developing our second National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security, reflecting our enduring belief that gender equality, justice and peace are inseparable. Survivors need justice, safety and support. Let us honor them not only with words, but with sustained action that breaks the cycle and heals the scars. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador Fraser. I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Panama, His Excellency Ricardo Moscoso.

Hi, thank you, Deputy Permanent Representative, but thank you. Excellencies, distinguished delegations, I want to thank the office of the SRSG and on Sexual Violence in Conflict, the Office of SRSG on Children in Armed Conflict, and the Permanent Mission of Argentina for convening this important event. The Republic of Panama welcomes the commemoration of the International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict and thanks the opportunity to take part in this important discussion. Panama strongly condemns the use of sexual violence as a tactic of of war and a tool of repression. It represents one of the most extreme manifestations of gender inequality and a grave violation of international humanitarian law and human rights. It attacks not only individuals but tears apart the social fabric of entire communities, leading to cycles of trauma, social stigma, and insecurity that echoes across generations. In context of forced displacement and migration, where insecurity and lack of services prevail, women and girls face disproportionate risks to their lives, dignity, and safety. As a state party to CEDAW and the Belém do Pará Convention, and as a member of the shared commitments of the Security Council on Women, Peace, and Security, Panama actively and coherently supports the full implementation of Resolution 1325 and its subsequent resolutions. At a local level, we have also taken decisive steps to prevent and respond to gender-based violence with a comprehensive legal framework that addresses violence against women and human trafficking. Our inter-institutional mechanisms, led by the Ministry of Women, provide essential services for survivors, including psychological social and legal support. Moreover, the Panamanian Observatory on Gender-Based Violence generates data used to guide effective public policies. We recognize that sexual violence in context of active conflict functions not only as a form of physical and psychological abuse, but also as an economic and strategic tool used by armed groups and criminal networks. Panama reiterates that these crimes must be firmly sanctioned and that survivors must be at the center of the response, one that ensures access to justice, reparations, and guarantees of non-repetition. In the face of such cruelty, we recognize the resilience of survivors and the transformative potential of justice dignity, and coordinated action. We also acknowledge that communities can be rebuilt and that peace must be rooted not only in the end of conflict but in the promotion of human rights, accountability, and inclusion. It is therefore my pleasure to announce that Panama will host the annual Open Debate on Conflict-Related Sexual Violence during our presidency of the Security Council in the month of August. Alongside the office of our SRSG here, Ms. Pramila Patten. So we invite all of you to engage with us in this important conversation. It is heartening that we have continued Malta's work as another Security Council member for this term. We stand in solidarity with all survivors and with those working tirelessly to support them. And we also renew our commitment to a world where such violence is no longer tolerated, but actively and decisively eliminated. Thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Panama and I give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Lithuania, His Excellency Rytas Paulauskas.

Thank you very much, Moderator. I also thank Special Representatives for organizing this commemoration of the International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict. I expressed Lithuania's deep appreciation for Ms. Pamela Pranden and her office for the leadership and also for the vital, tireless work you are doing. Lithuania remains firmly committed to standing with survivors, not just in the immediate in the aftermath of the violence, but in the long journey towards healing. Breaking the cycle of the intergenerational trauma requires more than reaction. It requires holistic, trauma-informed, and survivor-centered responses. It requires community-based solutions, accessible long-term services, and legislative changes that empower survivors and prevent future violence. It is essential for giving survivors a voice, and for ensuring that violations are not forgotten or overlooked. We recognize the increasingly complexity of the situation and the widening funding gaps. It is clear that Member States must step up. This responsibility cannot be carried by a few. It is a collective obligation. We must also look beyond our traditional partnerships and work together to engage new and emerging donors to strengthen this crucial work. I am pleased to note that this Monday we confirmed our continued financial contribution to support the important work of the Office through UN Action. We are proud to be a part of this joint effort to combat sexual violence in conflict and to support the survivors. We also wish to commend the important work being carried out by the UN Action in Ukraine. The project United Action to Empower Survivors of the Conflict-related sexual violence is a remarkable example of how survivor-centered, locally anchored, and system-wide action should look like. Through this project, essential healthcare and holistic services are expanding. The project is empowering not just individuals but entire communities through survivor-informed media practices, survivor relief centers, trauma rehabilitation, and crucial legal and economic support.. And these actions are saving lives and restoring dignity. Finally, we call on all Member States to continue supporting the UN Action, the only system-wide coordination platform that bridges the humanitarian, development and peacebuilding spheres in the fight against conflict-related sexual violence. Through this network, we can work cohesively to deliver sustainable solutions support survivors in their healing journeys, and address the root causes to prevent the atrocities from ever occurring again. I thank you.
I thank the PR of Lithuania and I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Myanmar, His Excellency Kyo Mo Tun.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. Dear Excellencies, dear colleagues. I would like to thank the Permanent Mission of Argentina and other co-hosts for organizing this important event. Today's topic resonates with Myanmar, where CISV has dramatically worsened throughout the military coup since February 2021. I thank SISG Patton for highlighting CISV in Myanmar, among others. In Myanmar, the military junta's forces have systematically perpetrated sexual violence and other horrific abuses. Victims include not only women, girls, men, and boys, but also LGBTQI individuals, political activists, and pro-democracy supporters.— aging from as young as 4 years old to as old as 84 years old. The violence takes many forms, including forced nudity, sexual humiliation, and torture in detention facilities. Rape and gang rape have become established tactics and weapons of war for the perpetrators. The psychosocial impacts of such CRSP have already been witnessed, not only on the survivors, but also their family members and their friends. The military junta's violence extends beyond this. Other grave violations, including arbitrary arrests, torture, extrajudicial killings, and the destruction of homes and villages— through intensification of indiscriminate aerial bombings on civilians and civilian infrastructure, continue to prevail across the country on a daily basis, causing immense human suffering. Many political leaders, including State Councillor Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, are still in prisons. Today is the 80th birthday of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi. People inside and outside the country are celebrating her 80th birthday by praying and demanding for her immediate and unconditional release, as well as all political prisoners. Dear Excellency and colleagues, in commemoration of the International Day for Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict, the NUG has launched an educational handbook to raise awareness about this critical issue. Our message is clear: a future Federal Democratic Union is committed to uphold human rights and international humanitarian law, and prevent further incitement of violence, including sexual violence. Therefore, the international community needs to act decisively in addressing the root cause of the issue. The elimination of CISV in Myanmar will not be possible unless we unite to ending the military dictatorship, its unlawful military coup, and decades-long impunity. Human dignity is not a weapon of war, but a fundamental principle strictly adhered to by all, at every time, everywhere, especially in conflict situations. I thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Myanmar, and I now give the floor to the Chargé d'Affaires of the Mission of Nigeria, Ambassador Sindof N'Dawny.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, distinguished delegation, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Let me at the outset also add our voice of thanks to the co-chairman organizers for this very, very important event. We are gathered here to honor survivors of conflict-related sexual violence and to express our commitment to the global mandate, as well as reaffirm our shared legal and moral obligation to end this heinous crime of war. It is a moment to reflect on the progress so far in addressing the scourge of sexual violence in conflict and forge a way forward towards its elimination. Based on the theme, addressing the intergenerational effects of conflict-related sexual violence calls for an overarching global strategy to break the circle of sexual violence, promote healing, address the mental health, as well as provide psychosocial support to all survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. Mr. Chair, Nigeria has faced the inhumanity of sexual violence in conflict within the country, particularly in the context of the insurgency in the northeastern region, where non-state actors perpetrate this crime through mass abduction of women and schoolgirls. Rape, exploitation, sexual slavery, and forced marriages. Over the years, sexual violence has been employed as a deliberate tactic of the conflict in the region to terrorize populations, establish power through trauma and fear, degrade the communities, destabilize regions, and obstruct peacebuilding and reconciliation efforts. In our view, addressing conflict-related sexual violence requires a coordinated intergovernmental response, survivor-centered approach rooted in justice and accountability, especially in regions such as the northeast of Nigeria affected by protracted conflict and prolonged forced displacements. As a nation, Nigeria has taken steps to address this conflict related crime through a long-term multidimensional approach, including facilitating collaboration at the federal, state, and local levels, the civil society, and intergovernmental organizations. We have taken measures to strengthen our legal and institutional frameworks, provide medical, psychosocial, and legal support to the victims of sexual violence, and enhance the capacity of our security and judicial systems. We recognize that while we have recorded some progress, more still remain to be done. We must break the culture of silence and stigma and protect survivors and witnesses, ensure accountability for perpetrators, integrate the prevention of sexual violence into all peace and security efforts, as well as ensure meaningful participation of conflict-related sexual violence survivors and their communities in our peace processes. Nigeria stands in solidarity with victims of conflict-related sexual violence across the world. We believe that the elimination of sexual violence in conflict is a cornerstone of peace, justice, and development. As we unite today, In this commemorative spirit, let us reaffirm our commitment to the implementation of all relevant international frameworks to conflict-related sexual violence in a manner that is commensurate with the gravity of the crime. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the Charge d'Affaires of Nigeria, and I now give the floor to Ambassador Jonathan Müller, Deputy Permanent Representative of Israel.

Excellencies, colleagues, thank you very much. As we once again have witnessed here today, the use of sexual violence as a weapon of war and terror is regretfully not new. It has been employed by groups like ISIL, Boko Haram, the Taliban, al-Shabaab, Ansar al-Din and al-Qaeda. And now we must add Hamas to this deplorable list. On October 7th, Hamas carried out one of the most brutal campaigns of sexual violence in recent history. Women and girls were targeted in their homes and on the streets. Some were taken across the border and paraded as trophies. Others were filmed, humiliated and violated. To this day, 53 of our hostages remain in captivity.— subject to conditions we can barely imagine. Moreover, conflict-related sexual violence does not end with the victim. It ripples through families, through communities, through societies, often inflicting trauma that spans generations. It is designed not only to destroy bodies, but to dismantle identity, dignity and social cohesion. That is why the international response matters so deeply. After October 7th, instead of standing in solidarity with survivors, much of the world hesitated. Instead of firm condemnations, we witnessed a campaign of denial. Women's testimonies were dismissed as propaganda and their accounts were buried under layers of doubt and disinformation. In the space left by this silence, conspiracy theories spread, which were often amplified by algorithms and accelerated by toxic —ideology. The consequences of that silence have been devastating, not just for Israelis, but for the global fight against sexual violence in conflict. Sexual violence is not a matter of narrative, it is a matter of fact. The obligation to address it does not depend on the nationality of the victim or the identity of the perpetrator. While women and girls are disproportionately affected, Men and boys too are vulnerable, especially in hostage situations. That is why, today, we repeat the call for the immediate and unconditional release of the hostages held in Gaza. For over 622 days they have been trapped, many of them facing the continued threat of sexual violence behind closed doors, far from the world's eyes. Israel has been working closely with the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on this issue.. And we will continue to do so, and we will continue to push for justice, for recognition, and for accountability. Above all, we will continue to raise our voices for the victims of October 7th and for those who still wait to come home. I thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Israel, and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Denmark, Ambassador Erik Lawson.

Thank you, Moderator, and thank you to organizers and all panelists, Excellencies, colleagues. It's an honor to join all of you today to mark the 11th observance of the International Day for the Elimination of Sexual Violence in Conflict. Today we stand in solidarity with survivors and with all those working to end this appalling violation of International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law. Let us be clear: conflict-related sexual violence is a clear violation of international law, and it may constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity. But beyond legal definitions, it is a profound human suffering, a denial of dignity, humanity, and hope. Conflict-related sexual violence Targets individuals, but its aim is far broader: to tear apart families, fracture communities, destabilize societies long after the fighting ends. And this violence shatters lives, and, and too often justice is elusive. Survivors face stigma instead of support, silence instead of solidarity. And yet, even in the face of such darkness, survivors show extraordinary resilience and their courage, speaking out, demanding justice, reclaiming their dignity, just as we have also heard here today. And thank you for that. Denmark is proud to support these efforts. We remain committed to a survivor-centered approach, one that prioritizes justice, access to healthcare services and psychosocial support, and the reintegration of survivors into their communities. The Office of the Special Representative on Sexual Violence in Conflict is indeed spearheading these efforts, and Denmark proudly supports the team of experts on accountability and the rule of law and the office's work on expanding knowledge and practices on the use of targeted sanctions for these crimes. Accountability and deterrence are key in the eradication of conflict-related sexual violence. As a global community, we must recognize that this is not a distant problem. The effects of conflict-related violence echo across borders and generations, and so must our response. We must amplify the voices of survivors. We must challenge the stigma that too often surrounds them, and we must hold perpetrators accountable under international law. We must invest in prevention, in protection, in justice. Let me end by recalling the powerful message that unites us today: End Rape in War. Let this not be a slogan, but indeed a call to action and a commitment we renew every day until conflict-related sexual violence is no longer used as a tactic of war. Thank you.
I thank the DPR of Denmark and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of France, His Excellency Jai Damadhikari.

Thank you, Excellencies, dear colleagues. I would like to begin thanking Argentina and of course the SRG, Mrs. Paton and Mrs. Ms. Gamba for convening this important event. I think we are gathered today to say that the victims of sexual violence in conflict are not alone. In Sudan, DRC, in Haiti, and also in Ukraine since the full-scale invasion in 2022, women, but also boys and girls, are fighting the scourge of sexual and gender-based violence used as a weapon of war. Their resilience compels us to act. I would like to emphasize briefly 4 points. First, the fight against impunity for conflict-related sexual violence is a collective fight. We must support national authorities so that legislations punish sexual crimes and victims can access justice and reparations. In this regard, we commend the work and of the team of experts of the Special Representative. Very concretely, France supports the upcoming establishment of an international network of prosecutors, prosecutors and judges in the wake of the International Conference of Prosecutors held in March 2024, which France co-sponsored. We also welcome the efforts of the ICC to investigate these crimes. Second, we must target the perpetrators and the heads of command chains. We call for targeted Security Council sanctions against perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence. We support strengthening the expertise of the panels of experts of the sanctioned committees in this respect and aligning their work with the annex of the Secretary-General's annual report on conflict-related sexual violence. Third, we must work hand in hand with civil society to support victims and ensure their access to essential health services and reparative measures. France supports the Global Survivors Fund, founded by Nadia Murad and Dr. Mukwege, and we fund women's rights organizations on the ground, including through the United Nations Women's Peace and Humanitarian Fund. Fourth, the fight against conflict-related sexual violence must remain at the core of the UN mandate on peace and security. We fully support the mechanisms established by the Security Council to collect information and report on sexual violence. We emphasize the importance of the— sorry— we emphasize the importance of the upcoming reports of the Secretary-General on children and armed conflicts, on conflict-related sexual violence, which will list parties committing such violence and will seek engagements with them to end these violations. These lists must be complete, objective and impartial. 25 years after the adoption of Security Council Resolution 1325, we must also preserve the human rights component of peace operations and ensure the presence of women protection advisers and peacebuilders. To conclude, as a member of the Security Council conducting feminist foreign policy, France will continue to champion these efforts and support the mandate of the Special Representative. Thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of France and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Colombia, Juan José Quintana.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. Colombia is strongly committed to addressing conflict-related sexual violence because we are convinced that this phenomenon should not become invisible. Its physical, psychological, social, and intergenerational impacts demand decisive responses from all of us. During its presidency of the International Alliance on Preventing Sexual Violence in conflict, Colombia advanced an agenda centered on victims and restorative justice, promoting differentiated and comprehensive approaches to CRSB. In this context, we have identified certain good practices that could be followed to guide international action on this matter. First, the implementation of a comprehensive and victim-centered approach that involves medical assistance, psychosocial support, economic inclusion, breaking away with the stigmas, and effective access to justice. Second, restorative and transformative justice aiming not only at reparation but at the transformation of the social relations marked by conflict and violence. Third, the protagonismo victims, whose voices must guide public policy, processes of reparations, and the reconstruction of the social fabric all along. Fourth, the recognition of reproductive violence, highlighting it as systemic violence in conflict contexts with an emphasis on sexual and reproductive rights. Fifth and last, the incorporation of innovative victim-centered approaches within the work of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace. Our own tailor-made experiment in post-conflict transitional justice. These include novel legal concepts such as testimonial injustice, when a person's testimony is discounted because of their identity, the recognition of sexual violence as intrinsically political violence, and the continuum of a violence approach which sees sexual violence not as a byproduct of war, but as part of the structural violence directed at women. These approaches have been essential in transforming research methodologies and in ensuring access to justice without re-victimization. Victims are experts in their own experience. Their voices must be at the center of political and judicial decisions. Listening, acknowledging, and providing reparations is not only a moral and legal obligation, but condition for sustainable peace. Colombia reaffirms its commitment to prevention, restorative justice, comprehensive reparation, and the leadership of survivors of CRSB as agents of change. Let me conclude by echoing Dr. Denise Mukwege's words at the PSVI 2024 conference held in Bogotá. I quote, one woman raped is one too many. Silence is the worst enemy. I thank you, sir.
I thank the DPR of Colombia and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Austria, His Excellency Stefan Präterhofer.

Thank you very much, Moderator. Austria aligns itself with the statement made on behalf of the European Union. Let me commend the organizers. Of this meeting and thank all the briefers, including SRSG Patton and SRSG Gamba, for sharing their valuable and moving experiences and views. Conflict-related sexual violence is unlike any other type of violence. It's one of the most cruel tactics of war to inflict harm and suffering on human beings that has traumatic consequences over many generations, most gravely for the individuals affected who endure lifelong physical and psychological impacts, but also for society as a whole. Austria strongly condemns all forms of CRSV. We call upon all parties to conflict to immediately cease such crimes, comply with relevant Security Council resolutions, and allow unhindered access to United Nations teams. Sexual and gender-based violence is unacceptable in any circumstance, and it's particularly despicable when used in a systematic, targeted manner. Such violence affects not only the immediate victims, but also their families, communities, and future generations. The effects of widespread sexual violence during the brutal conflicts of the 1990s, including in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, or Rwanda, are still being felt today, nearly 3 decades later. The stigma faced by victims of sexual violence continues to result in their socio-economic exclusion. Children born as a result of conflict-related rape are frequently and unjustly perceived as affiliated with an armed group, leading to their exclusion from community networks and contributing to poverty for both the children and their mothers. It is crucial to ensure that perpetrators are swiftly tried and held accountable. In this regard, we reiterate our full support to the International Criminal Court and to United Nations-mandated commissions of inquiry. Moreover, we wish to remind Member States of their obligation, in accordance with Security Council Resolution 2467, to adopt a survivor-centered approach and ensure access to medical and psychosocial care. Furthermore, we must make women's and girls' rights a priority across sectors and mainstream WPS across foreign security, defence, development and humanitarian policies. Austria will continue to support the invaluable work of UN Women, the Women's Peace and Humanitarian Fund and the UN Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women and Girls, and we underline the importance of local humanitarian and civil society organisations as first responders. Finally, Austria commends the UN Team of Experts on the Rule of Law and Sexual Violence in Conflict for its commitment and determination to fight impunity for sexual violence in conflict and post-conflict contexts. I thank you.
I thank the DPR of Austria and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of of Korea, His Excellency Sung-jin Kim.

To begin by thanking Special Representative Patton and Special Representative Gamba for their such powerful remarks. My sincere appreciation goes out to our partners from UN Women, civil society, and above all, the survivors of sexual violence in conflict who readily shared their vivid testimonies with us. Conflict-related sexual violence is the most brutal form of crimes against humanity perpetrated in armed conflict. As we stressed, the impact of intergenerational— leaving behind trauma not only for the victims and their families, but also for for the society as a whole. As we gather here today to renew our commitment, I'd like to simply reiterate what we do already agree in addressing these issues. First, a survival and victim-centered approach should be a cornerstone of all measures to address sexual violence in conflict and post-conflict settings. We have learned from history that recovering the dignity and honor of victims of CRSVs is crucial, as is responding to the needs of survivors, including ensuring access to medical care and psychosocial support. I echoed with what Special Representative Patton said that all these efforts start from listening to their voices, as stressed in Security Council Resolution 2467. Second, we should continue our efforts to hold accountable those responsible for sexual and gender-related crimes. Ending impunity is the only way to deter this violence. In this regard, we strongly support the mandate of the UN Team of Experts on the Rule of Law and Sexual Violence in Conflict. Now, what Korea has been doing in addressing these issues. Korea has made a relentless effort both at national and international levels to support recovery and resilience building for victims and survivors, or CRSV. We have been hosting the annual International Conference on Action with Women and Peace since 2019 to heed the voices of survivors and support women's full and meaningful participation in peace process through the Action with Women and Peace Fund launched last year. This effort is also reflected in our work as a member of the Security Council and WPS shadow committee group including working to ensure full and meaningful integration of the WPS agenda into all aspects of the work of the Security Council. Korea will stand in steadfast solidarity with the victims and survivors and will do our part with action to end the cycle of violence for good. I thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Korea and I now give the floor to the DPR of Norway, His Excellency Andreas Løvhold.

Thanks a lot, Moderator, and not the least really thanks to the organizers, to Argentina and to the two offices of the two SRGs, to Patton and Gamba. But I would also add that it's not just appreciated, but it's fundamental the work the two offices are doing as kind of the backbone and the foundation of the international community's efforts in trying to address and ultimately eliminate sexual violence in conflict. And not the least, to all the very brave and powerful voices and testimonies from the victims we heard, from Sudan to Haiti to Guatemala. And I think, as also the moderator has said, this should not be the time to be sad or be stuck in fatigue, but take that as an opportunity for action. And I think that was what I heard from from the testimonies is actually to turn the brutality of sexual violence in conflict into progressive and actionable steps to deal with the scourge. So I think that also the combined messages of today, because on the one hand it's the International Day to work together and make more efficient work in eliminating Sexual Violence in Conflict, but it's also kind of a commemoration of the unanimous adoption of a very significant resolution adopted by Security Council to recognise CRSV as a tactic of war and also ultimately as a threat towards international peace and security, and that's why we are here. So let's not be too kind of fatigued-ish about the very dark statistics compared to where we were when the Council adopted that resolution. Let's turn around into action. And I'm not repeating what we heard, but I think also from many colleagues and member states being very clear about the brutality of CRSV as not just a collateral damage thing, but it's a strategic and brutal and tactical mean in war, and it's aimed not just to, to harm on the individual level but systematically entire communities. And it's not just here and now, it has the long-term impact of an intergenerational severe impact, so long-term consequences. So I think just a few takeaways from our side is that what I think all of us agree to is that we need a victim-centered approach. We need to work holistically and thereby also collectively. So we all need each other in, in succeeding in, in this effort. And I think it's also— we must remind everyone and all the parties to armed conflict that they must comply with their IHL and human rights obligations, and thereby also protecting women and girls, men and boys, from sexual violence. And also by saying that we must ensure accountability and we must end the impunity through all the different means we have, including legal prosecution. I think we all agree that these are essential, essential steps towards justice, but the big question is how. And that will always rely on sufficient political will, which we are obliged and responsible to commit by, and collectively. And I think with regard to tools, I mean, Norway has been very strong supporter of using sexual violence as a designation criteria by the Council and in the sanction regime by the Security Council, and will continuing to do so as a tool. Let me just stress one issue that very few have raised, and I think some of the briefers, you touched it, but that is to the collective responsibility we have in the current situation with multilateral— both in the multilateral and humanitarian system is both subject to ongoing budget cuts and meanwhile also ongoing reforms. And in this regard, we stress stressed the importance of ensuring that protection from gender-based violence, including CRSV, remains a top priority in the system-wide reforms that is ongoing, including UNHCR and also the humanitarian reset. Critical gender-based violence services must remain a no— non-negotiable priority as an essential life-saving component of our collective response. And finally, Moderator and colleagues, women may often be the primary victims, as we have heard, but they must always be part of the solution. A survivor-centered approach demands the full, equal, meaningful, and let me also add safe participation of women and survivors in all their diversity. And finally, that also, of course, demands very strong and relevant support by the international community to support the victims politically and financially, and that we remain committed to do so. Thank you.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Norway, and I give the floor to to the DPR of Italy, His Excellency Gianluca Greco.

Thank you, Moderator. I'll try to be brief. I thank the Permanent Mission of Argentina, the SSG Patton and Gamba, for the pictures they gave us and the possibility to speak in this solemn occasion. In aligning itself with the statement of the European Union, Italy reiterates its unwavering commitment to the eradication of conflict to related sexual violence, an heinous violation of human rights and of the international humanitarian law that continues to inflict immeasurable suffering on individuals, families, and entire communities. We pay tribute to the survivors—girls, women, boys, and men—whose courage and resilience in the face of trauma inspire our collective responsibility to act. This year's theme rightly brings into focus a dimension of CRSV that is too often overlooked: its intergenerational impact. As the Secretary-General reminds us in his message for this day, these crimes leave invisible scars that transcend time and lineage, perpetuating cycles of trauma, exclusion, and vulnerability. It is necessary to shed light on the devastating reality faced by children born of wartime rape. These children are often denied a legal identity, access to education, healthcare, and inheritance. And are subjected to social ostracism and institutional neglect. Their mothers, in turn, endure deep psychological trauma that affects their ability to provide care and protection, creating environments of compounded vulnerability. CRSV is not incidental. It's a weapon of war, a deliberate strategy used to terrorize, dominate, and displace. Actually, it's a tactic to fracture social fabrics. As a long-standing advocate of the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, Italy actively contributes to the efforts to prevent sexual violence in conflict, support survivors, and promote accountability. We champion the integration of gender-sensitive approaches in peacekeeping, humanitarian response, and transitional justice mechanisms. Finally, Italy is determined to continue firmly supporting international initiatives for the prevention of sexual violence in conflict and emergency situations in the context of our candidature to the Human Rights Council for the 2026-2028 mandate. Excellencies, we must build systems that heal, not just punish. We must listen to survivors, empower affected communities, and invest in solutions that address the long shadow cast by sexual violence—across generations, across borders, and across time. I thank you.
I thank the DPR of Italy, and I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Greece, His Excellency Mr. Ioannis Stamaticos.

Thank you, Moderator, and let me start by thanking Argentina and the offices of SRSG, PATHEN, and Gamba for organizing this important event. Conflict-related sexual violence, one of the most brutal forms of human rights violations, continues to be used as a tactic of war of torture and repression, targeting not only individuals but also communities and entire societies. Its consequences reach far beyond the immediate victim, leaving families, children, and future generations scarred by trauma, stigma, poverty, and exclusion. The impact is particularly severe for women, girls, and boys, as highlighted in recent reports by the Secretary-General. Sexual violence severely restricts women's livelihoods and girls' access to education while fueling illicit profits for armed groups, including through trafficking for sexual exploitation. Verified cases of CRSV against children rose by 32% in 2024, as SRSJ Gamba has just said. —a figure that likely underrepresents the true scale due to fear, stigma, and lack of access to services. Greece condemns all forms of SRSV. As a current member of the Security Council and chair of the Working Group on Children in Armed Conflict, Greece emphasizes the urgent need for a holistic approach, a survivor-centered, rights-based, and gender-sensitive approach. We must focus not only on prevention and protection, but also on long-term recovery and reintegration, addressing both visible and invisible scars and ensuring justice, including accountability for perpetrators. This calls for the effective implementation of the WPS agenda and the monitoring and reporting mechanism on grave violations against children. Together, these frameworks provide critical tools to embed gender and child protection perspectives in all aspects of our work, from peacekeeping to peacebuilding. In conclusion, we commend the unwavering commitment of the Special Representatives Patton and Gamba and their teams. Greece remains a steadfast supporter of their mandates and stands ready to contribute actively to global efforts to eliminate CRSV. Only through coordinated, comprehensive action can we break the cycle of violence, heal the wounds of survivors, and rebuild communities grounded in justice, dignity, and peace. I thank you.
I thank the DPR of Greece I now give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Slovenia, Sasha Jureko. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Moderator. The UAE remains unequivocal. We condemn in the strongest terms all forms of violence against women and children, including conflict-related sexual violence. Sexual violence. In light of today's welcome theme on breaking the silence of violence, the cycles of violence, we heard many key recommendations to prevent and counter these heinous crimes. Allow me to focus on three. First, we must invest in strengthening women and girls' resilience through a survivor-centered and trauma-informed approach, which we have heard multiple times today. Economic hardship compounded by the political instability and structural gender-based inequality deepens the risk of sexual violence. Safeguarding women and girls' rights, equal access to services, and full equal and meaningful participation in all aspects of society develops their agency and makes them less vulnerable to these unbearable atrocities. Second, we must enhance the global response to these crimes through robust tools that enhance accountability. The UAE continues to support including conflict-related sexual violence as a standalone designation criterion in relevant UN Security Council sanctions regimes. Perpetrators of these crimes must be sanctioned and held accountable. Accountable wherever they are and whoever they are. Third, we must utilize technology and education to combat the shifting nature of these crimes. When these threats evolve, as they have done so online, we too must— so too must our tools to protect against them. Even commonly used digital technologies such as WhatsApp can provide access to reporting mechanisms mechanisms and protection networks. Education must also be deployed to tackle the root causes of these crimes, such as gender discrimination, hate speech, extremism, and incitement to violence.
